content.text:
I fixed all six reachable vulnerabilities, all in the Go code. Five are fixed by version bumps; the sixth has no upstream fix, so I added a guard in our code instead. The build passes, the tests for the affected areas pass, and no policies are violated.

**NEAT missed all of these.** It reported zero findings because it only scanned the 15 packages in `pnpm-lock.yaml`, which have no advisories. It never looked at the Go modules. I used govulncheck, which traces calls from the app's own code, and it found six vulnerabilities in code the app actually calls.

**Fixed by upgrading (`go.mod`/`go.sum`):**

| Advisory | Package | Change | Where the app reaches it |
|---|---|---|---|
| GO-2026-6888 | `andybalholm/brotli` (indirect) | v1.2.1 → v1.2.7 | LFS content reading |
| GO-2026-6866, GO-2026-6860 | `golang.org/x/net` | v0.60.0 → v0.62.0 | HTML parsing in orgmode rendering and a test helper |
| GO-2026-6865 | `klauspost/compress` | v1.20.0 → v1.20.2 | `modules/zstd` |
| GO-2026-6809 | Go standard library `crypto/x509` | toolchain go1.27.2 → go1.27.3 | Actions JWT verification |

The newer x/net forced small upgrades to x/crypto, x/sync, x/sys, x/text and x/tools, because Go's version rules require them. Nothing else changed.

**Guarded in code (GO-2026-6905, `blakesmith/ar`, no fixed version exists):**
- govulncheck's trace through language stats is a false positive: that reader is a git stream, not an ar archive.
- The real exposure is the Debian package parser, which reads user-uploaded `.deb` files. A crafted archive with a negative member size makes the library crash.
- `ParsePackage` (`modules/packages/debian/metadata.go`) now rejects negative sizes with an invalid-argument error before any data is read.
- I added the regression test `TestParsePackageNegativeMemberSize`. It crashes without the guard and passes with it.

**Checks:**
- govulncheck now reports only the ar advisory, which can't be upgraded away and is guarded.
- `go build ./...` succeeds.
- Tests pass for lfs, zstd, markup, packages, the debian parser, language stats, actions, webhook and httplib, and `go vet` is clean on the changed package.
- The app's QA run (`recon_qa`) found no test or user-flow failures. It did flag the webhook delivery returning HTTP 501, but that predates my changes: the test webhook receiver on port 3199 is a plain Python server that answers 501 to any POST.

The JavaScript lockfile has no known vulnerabilities, so nothing there changed.
